939.title: The Ring of the Dove
939.hook: Ibn Hazm, jurist and poet, writes a book on love
939.howItsDone: The Ring of the Dove is read today as a classic of Arabic prose about love; readers often note that its author, Ibn Hazm, was also a jurist, and that the book closes with chapters on avoiding sin and practicing self-restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ziryab, the singer from Baghdad who taught Cordoba new music and new meals. Your line was: music and manners.

A man who writes on Islamic law, rigorous and famously sharp in argument, sits down to write about something else. A friend has asked him, the book's opening tells us: what is love, what are its signs, what happens to people inside it? Law books are serious, and this would be a book of glances, letters, messengers, jealousy, waiting at doors. He wrote it anyway, with poems of his own scattered through it. The writer was Ibn Hazm of Cordoba. The book: The Ring of the Dove.
screen: `A JURIST GETS A QUESTION.` → `WHAT IS LOVE?` → `HE WRITES IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Ibn Hazm was a jurist who held to the plain, outward meaning of the Qur'an and the hadith, and he argued hard for it. That's what makes the book surprising. He doesn't scold love as a weakness. He studies it, the way he'd study any question. And he says early on that love in itself is not forbidden by religion or condemned by the law; what it leads to is a separate question. The book reads like a field guide. The signs of love: eyes that keep returning to one face, a conversation steered back to one name. Falling in love at a single look, and falling slowly over years. Keeping a secret, the friend who carries messages, faithfulness, separation, grief. He tells stories from his own life and from people he knew, honestly enough that some still sting. Where does love come from? Ibn Hazm leans toward the soul. He points to the Qur'an's account of humanity created from a single soul, with its mate made from it. Love, in his reading, has something to do with souls recognizing each other. The Qur'an says of spouses, in Pickthall's translation: "He ordained between you love and mercy." And the ending is the jurist's signature. The last chapters turn to the ugliness of sin and the beauty of self-restraint. He doesn't pretend desire is tame; he just won't let the book end without asking what love is for. A book on love.
screen: `A JURIST OF THE PLAIN MEANING.` · `A FIELD GUIDE TO LOVE'S SIGNS.` · `SOULS THAT RECOGNIZE EACH OTHER.` · `IT ENDS WITH SELF-RESTRAINT.` · then, large: `A BOOK ON LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let one person you love come to mind, a parent, a partner, a child, a friend you've drifted from, and notice one specific thing about them the way Ibn Hazm notices: a habit, a phrase they always use, a moment you've never mentioned. Then find the first plain sentence you'd write to them. If you pray, remember them in your prayer; if you don't, just keep their face in mind.

940.title: Ibn Rushd
940.hook: the judge and philosopher of Cordoba, known in Europe as Averroes
940.howItsDone: Some students of philosophy and theology read Ibn Rushd's Decisive Treatise and his reply to al-Ghazali side by side with al-Ghazali's own work; Muslim scholars hold differing views on the place of philosophy in religious learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Hazm and The Ring of the Dove, a jurist's book on love that ends in self-restraint. Your line was: a book on love.

Is it allowed, by the religious law itself, to study philosophy? Or is it required? A judge of Cordoba set out to answer that in a short, tightly argued book. As a judge he ruled on inheritance and contracts. As a philosopher he wrote line-by-line commentaries on Aristotle, and those commentaries traveled north into Latin, where readers knew him as Averroes. In Arabic he was Ibn Rushd, and he thought the Qur'an itself was sending people to think.
screen: `ALLOWED, OR REQUIRED?` → `A JUDGE WHO READ ARISTOTLE.` → `IN LATIN: AVERROES.`

segments.voice: The book is often called The Decisive Treatise, and it starts from the Qur'an, not from Aristotle. Ibn Rushd gathers verses that tell people to reflect. One ends, in Pickthall's translation: "So learn a lesson, O ye who have eyes!" Cross over in your mind from what you see to what it means. If the Qur'an commands that, he argues, those able to reason carefully about the world are being asked to do it, and the best tools for careful reasoning deserve to be learned, even from people outside the faith. His homely picture: if someone before you already made the knife for the sacrifice, you use the knife; you don't ask whether its maker shared your religion. You check that it cuts properly. Then the harder question: what if reasoning and scripture seem to clash? His answer: truth does not oppose truth. Where a proven conclusion meets the outward sense of a verse, the verse has a deeper reading that agrees with it, and those trained to look should look. Not everyone agreed. Before him, the theologian al-Ghazali had written The Incoherence of the Philosophers, arguing that some of their conclusions went beyond what reason could prove and against what faith teaches. Ibn Rushd answered with The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Muslims still read both, and still argue the question in both directions. What Ibn Rushd left on the table is one conviction: the mind is not an intruder in the house of faith. Reason as a gift.

segments.voice: Aristotle's Metaphysics, a book Ibn Rushd commented on, opens by saying that human beings, by nature, desire to know. Turn that line over slowly: what did you want to know today, even something small, like how a word is spelled or why the sky looked that color? Let one honest question rise and stay with it; if you pray, hold it in your prayer, and if you don't, just keep it in view.

941.title: Ibn Arabi
941.hook: the mystic born in Murcia, who traveled east to Damascus
941.howItsDone: Some Sufi orders study Ibn Arabi's works closely and visit his tomb in Damascus; other Muslim scholars have criticized parts of his teaching, and the debate over him continues.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Rushd, the judge of Cordoba who argued that careful reasoning is a duty. Your line was: reason as a gift.

Yesterday's philosopher asks to meet a boy. The boy, in his own later telling, is barely grown, and people have been talking about him. Ibn Rushd rises to greet him and asks, more or less: is what you have found by inner opening the same as what we find by reasoning? The boy says yes. Ibn Rushd looks pleased. Then the boy says no. And between that yes and that no, the boy reports, the old philosopher went pale. The boy was Ibn Arabi, and the story is his own.

Ibn Arabi was born in Murcia, in al-Andalus, and never really stopped traveling. He went east, to Mecca, where he began a vast book called The Meccan Openings, and on through the cities of the Muslim world until he settled in Damascus, where he is buried. People called him al-Shaykh al-Akbar: the greatest master. Begin with a verse he and other Sufis return to. In Pickthall's translation: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." In his reading, if God's face is wherever you turn, then the world is full of signs, and every moment can be a meeting. Elsewhere the Qur'an says of each person, "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." For Ibn Arabi, knowing that nearness is not a conclusion you reason your way to. It is opened in you, the inner opening behind his no to Ibn Rushd. Reason goes far, in his view, but there is a kind of knowing it can't hand you. Now the honest part. His books are dense and daring, and Muslims have read them in sharply different ways. Among his Sufi readers he is treasured. Some scholars, Ibn Taymiyya among them, attacked parts of his teaching as error. Others defended him as a master misunderstood. That argument is still going, so today's line comes with two words attached on purpose. The greatest master, some say.

If you pray, bring the mystery into your prayer; if you don't, just keep it company.

942.title: Neighbors in al-Andalus
942.hook: Muslims, Jews and Christians shared cities and learning, alongside real tension and times of persecution
942.howItsDone: Muslims, Jews and Christians today remember al-Andalus in different ways; historians describe both its shared learning and its inequality and episodes of violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Arabi, the mystic from Murcia who answered the philosopher yes, and then no. Your line was: the greatest master, some say.

A general sits in an army camp and writes a poem. In Hebrew. He is Samuel ibn Naghrela, a Jew who serves a Muslim king of Granada as vizier, the chief minister, and leads that king's troops in the field. His Hebrew poems move in the meters of Arabic verse, and some were written on campaign: the night before a battle, the fear, the thanks for coming home alive. A Jewish commander, a Muslim court, Hebrew words in Arabic rhythms. That's one face of al-Andalus. His son's story shows the other, and today needs both.
screen: `A JEWISH VIZIER WRITES A POEM.` → `HEBREW IN ARABIC METERS.` → `HIS SON'S STORY IS THE OTHER FACE.`

segments.voice: Start with the frame. The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, and under Muslim rule in al-Andalus they lived as protected communities, with their own worship, clergy and courts. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits a Muslim neighbor didn't. Protection and inequality, in the same arrangement. Now the sharing. At the court of Abd al-Rahman the Third, a Jewish physician named Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a trusted diplomat. Jewish poets, Samuel among them, wrote Hebrew verse in the patterns of Arabic poetry. Philosophers of all three communities argued over the same Greek books, read in Arabic. Now the other side, said just as plainly. In Cordoba, some Christians who publicly denounced Islam were executed, and their community remembered them as martyrs. In Granada, a mob turned on the city's Jews, and among the dead was the vizier Joseph, Samuel's own son. Later, under the Almohads, Jews and Christians faced pressure to convert, and some fled; the family of the Jewish scholar Maimonides was among them. Christian kingdoms to the north, meanwhile, pushed south by war. So which was it, harmony or persecution? Both, at different times, in different cities, under different rulers. The Qur'an gives a reason for difference, in Pickthall's words: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Knowing one another includes the hard chapters. Shared, and not simple.

943.title: The Alhambra
943.hook: the red palace of Granada, walls covered with the words, no victor but Allah
943.howItsDone: Visitors to the Alhambra, Muslim and not, read the motto 'no victor but God' carved throughout its walls; Muslims often say that victory comes only from God, echoing the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Samuel ibn Naghrela and the neighbors of al-Andalus, sharing cities and words alongside inequality and violence. Your line was: shared, and not simple.

Stand in a courtyard in Granada and look closely at the wall. What looks like lace from a few steps back turns out, up close, to be writing: Arabic letters carved into plaster, woven through vines and stars. Some of it is the Qur'an. Some is poetry, praising the very room you're standing in. And again and again, one short sentence, small enough to fit in a corner and patient enough to fill a palace. Wa la ghaliba illa Allah. There is no victor but God.
screen: `LACE THAT TURNS OUT TO BE WRITING.` → `QUR'AN, POETRY, AND ONE SENTENCE.` → `NO VICTOR BUT GOD.`

segments.voice: The Alhambra sits on a hill above Granada. Its name is said to mean the red one, for the color of its walls. It was the palace of the Nasrid rulers of Granada. By then their map had shrunk: the Christian kingdoms had taken city after city, and Granada was what remained. That makes the motto worth hearing twice. People tell a story about it. The dynasty's founder came home from a battle, and the crowd hailed him as the victor. His answer, so the story goes, was the sentence that would cover his family's palace: no victor but God. Nobody can confirm the scene, but the sentence is carved there for anyone to read. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an word for word, but it leans on one. In Pickthall's translation: "Victory cometh only from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." A ruler writing that on his own walls says something odd for a ruler: the win is not mine; the throne answers to someone else. Then the craft. The writing doesn't sit on top of the decoration; it is the decoration. Letters climb, interlace, turn into borders. Geometry repeats without ending. Some poems speak in the room's own voice, as if the building were talking. A palace that keeps reminding its owners who owns it. No victor but Allah.

segments.voice: Picture a wall where one sentence is carved over and over among leaves and stars, until your eye stops seeing the pattern and starts reading it. Then bring to mind something you've won lately, a deadline met, an argument settled, a good day, and hold it lightly beside the sentence: no victor but God. If you pray, let those words rest on your breath; if you don't, notice how it feels to hold a win more loosely.

944.title: 1492 and after
944.hook: Granada falls, and the Muslims of Spain are later forced to convert or leave
944.howItsDone: The loss of al-Andalus and the expulsion of the Moriscos are remembered in Muslim histories, poetry and sermons; some families in North Africa trace their roots to the Moriscos.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alhambra, the red palace of Granada whose walls repeat one sentence. Your line was: no victor but allah.

South of Granada there's a mountain pass whose name is really a story: the sigh of the Moor. People tell that the sultan who handed Granada over, Abu Abdallah, whom the Spanish called Boabdil, rode out with his household, stopped at that pass, turned for one last look at the city and the red palace, and wept. Whether he wept there, nobody can say for certain. What came after his surrender is better documented, and it is harder to hear.
screen: `THE SIGH OF THE MOOR.` → `ONE LAST LOOK BACK.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Granada did not fall in a final battle. It was surrendered by treaty to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, and the treaty made promises: Muslims could keep their mosques, their faith, their law, their property. Those promises did not last. Before long the authorities were pressing Muslims to be baptized, and in time, across Spain, the choice became baptism or exile. Families who stayed, because home was home, were baptized, and came to be called Moriscos. Some became sincere Christians. Others kept Islam in secret, praying behind closed doors, teaching children quietly. And they wrote. Some Moriscos wrote Spanish in Arabic letters, copying prayers, stories of the prophets and rules of worship in a script their neighbors couldn't read. A language hiding inside another, so that faith could survive in a kitchen. The suspicion never lifted. There were rebellions, crushed. In the end the Moriscos as a whole, even those who were truly Christian, were expelled from Spain, crossing to North Africa and beyond. Their neighbors had been through it already. In the same year Granada surrendered, the Jews of Spain were ordered to convert or leave, and Jewish families left. Two communities, the same choice. This closes the walk through al-Andalus, and this ending belongs in the story too, beside the arches and the books. Remember the Moriscos.
screen: `SURRENDERED, WITH PROMISES.` · `BAPTISM OR EXILE.` · `SPANISH IN ARABIC LETTERS.` · `EXPELLED, AS THE JEWS HAD BEEN.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE MORISCOS.`

segments.voice: Think of a family made to leave a home they loved, the Moriscos at a harbor, or people forced from their homes today, and picture one ordinary thing they had to leave behind: a door key, a kitchen, a tree in a yard. Stay with that one thing. If you pray, remember them in whatever words are already yours; if you don't, keep them company in your attention.
Moriscos. The Muslims who stayed in Spain after Granada surrendered in fourteen ninety-two, forced to convert and, in the end, expelled. Today's word.
Your line: remember the moriscos. Faith survived in kitchens and in hidden letters. See you tomorrow.

945.title: Fatimah al-Fihri's Qarawiyyin
945.hook: a woman in Fez spends her inheritance on a mosque that becomes a place of learning
945.howItsDone: The Qarawiyyin in Fez is still a working mosque and a center of Islamic learning, and Muslims often cite Fatimah al-Fihri as an example of charity that keeps giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Moriscos. Granada surrendered, promises broke, and they were forced to convert and then expelled. Your line was: remember the moriscos.

An inheritance arrives. A father has died, and his daughter now has money of her own. A house, a business, a cushion for bad years? In Fez, in Morocco, a woman named Fatimah al-Fihri, whose family had come to the city from Kairouan, the chronicle says, chose a mosque. It would become the Qarawiyyin, and it would not stay only a mosque. The path crosses the strait to North Africa.
screen: `AN INHERITANCE ARRIVES.` → `SHE CHOOSES A MOSQUE.` → `IT WON'T STAY ONLY A MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Much of the story comes from a later chronicle of Fez, which tells it simply. Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad al-Fihri, was a devout woman. She spent what she inherited on building the mosque, from the ground up. Tradition adds that she fasted the whole time the building went on. And the chronicle says her sister Maryam did the same across the river, building a mosque for the other half of the city. Two sisters, two inheritances, two mosques. Why would someone do this? A hadith fits her story. Sahih Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in substance: when a person dies, their deeds end except for three things. Charity that keeps flowing. Knowledge people go on benefiting from. A good child who prays for them. Fatimah's mosque became the first two at once. Prayer filled it, and then teaching did. Scholars taught the Qur'an, law, grammar, and later much more, and students came from far away to sit in its circles. Over time it grew into what Fez now calls the University of al-Qarawiyyin. So the line isn't an exaggeration, just a long view. Look back over this week, and it's full of builders: a jurist who wrote on love, a judge who defended reason, a mystic, neighbors who built a shared and fragile culture, a palace that credited God with every win, a people who kept faith in hiding. And now a daughter with an inheritance. She founded a university.
screen: `A DAUGHTER'S INHERITANCE.` · `TWO SISTERS, TWO MOSQUES.` · `CHARITY THAT KEEPS FLOWING.` · `FROM PRAYER HALL TO UNIVERSITY.` · then, large: `SHE FOUNDED A UNIVERSITY.`

Qarawiyyin. The mosque Fatimah al-Fihri built in Fez with her inheritance, which grew into a university. Today's word.
